summary: Describes how subnet gateways can use the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) to let hosts on connected subnets communicate without knowing subnets exist. This technique is known as Proxy ARP.

eli5.summary: A receptionist answers the phone on behalf of someone in another office, so callers don't need to know there is a second office. Proxy ARP lets a router do this for computers.

questions: how do transparent subnet gateways work
when would i use proxy arp
why did proxy arp fade from use
subtitle: Letting routers pretend to be destination hosts on the same network.

tldr.problem: Hosts on different physical networks need to talk to each other, but network administrators can hide the existence of multiple subnets to keep systems simple. Without a trick, the systems would not know the correct route.
tldr.mechanism: A gateway running Proxy ARP watches for address-resolution broadcasts and, when a host on one subnet asks for the address of a host on another subnet, the gateway answers as if it were that host—telling the questioner to send traffic to the gateway instead.
tldr.outcome: The scheme is simple, requires no changes to hosts, and works well in controlled networks, but later protocols like subnetting and IP routing replaced it for larger deployments.

today: RFC 1027 is an Informational RFC describing a technique that was useful in the 1980s but is not commonly used today. Modern networks use standard subnetting (RFC 950) and dynamic routing protocols instead, which provide better scalability and control.

sections.title: Transparent Subnets Without Host Changes
sections.content:
RFC 1027 describes Proxy ARP, a technique that lets subnet gateways forward traffic between physical networks without requiring hosts on those networks to know subnets exist. When the University of Texas needed to split a large Ethernet into smaller segments, they could not modify the half-dozen or more operating systems already running on the hosts. Proxy ARP solved this by having gateways answer ARP requests on behalf of distant hosts, making the separate physical networks appear as one.

The protocol is often called the "ARP hack" because it bends the normal rules of the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) in a simple but effective way. It requires only that the gateways run new code; the hosts themselves need no changes.
sections.eli5: Instead of teaching every computer about subnets, a router sits in the middle and lies for computers on the far side of the network. It tells computers asking for a far-away address that it has that address, then forwards the traffic for them.

sections.title: How Proxy ARP Works
sections.content:
The mechanism is straightforward. When host A broadcasts an ARP request asking "Who has the address for host B", the ARP gateway listens. If host B is on a different physical network than host A (but reachable via the gateway), the gateway responds that host B's network address is actually the gateway's own address. Host A caches this and sends future packets to the gateway. The gateway then forwards the packets to host B using its routing tables. When host B replies, the same process happens in reverse.

For this to work, the gateway must not reply if the request and target are on the same physical network (or the same incoming and outgoing interface), because the destination should answer for itself. The gateway must also reject requests across different IP networks and requests for broadcast addresses, to prevent spoofing attacks and the "Chernobyl effect" where every host on a network replies to a broadcast simultaneously.
sections.eli5: When a computer asks for an address, the router answers "I have it, send to me" and then passes the message along. The computer thinks the far-away address is right next to it.

sections.title: Implementation in 4.3BSD
sections.content:
The protocol was implemented as an addition to 4.3BSD Unix with roughly 110 lines of kernel code. Most of the code lives in the generic Ethernet interface module, if_ether.c. The core logic is a routine called if_subarp (about 60 lines) that performs sanity checks and determines whether the gateway should respond to an ARP request. Code in ip_output also fixes broadcast addresses so that hosts without subnet support recognize them correctly.

A key implementation detail: the default route must not be used when checking the routing table for Proxy ARP replies. If it were, the gateway would answer every ARP request, which would fail because the default route's destination would not understand subnet routing. The implementation also needs special handling for multiple subnets on a single physical network (phantom subnets) and for the four different broadcast address conventions in use at the time: all-ones, all-zeros, and subnet-based variants.
sections.eli5: The code that makes it work is small—about 110 lines added to the operating system. It sits in the router's network code and intercepts address requests to decide whether to answer for a far-away computer.

sections.title: Design Trade-offs and Limitations
sections.content:
Proxy ARP trades simplicity for robustness. Its main strength is that it requires no changes to hosts or the address resolution protocol itself. No new routing table entries or ARP cache entries are needed in the gateway; only the hosts' ARP caches grow. The technique works best in a tree-structured network of subnets, where routing loops are prevented by careful administration.

Multiple gateways can serve the same route, and the first ARP reply wins, providing simple load balancing. However, the approach does not scale to large networks with many subnets and gateways. Also, all gateways must use identical network masks on every interface, or hosts will fail to find each other. The technique is most useful as a temporary measure or in small, controlled networks—which is why later standards like RFC 950 (subnetting) and routing protocols replaced it.
sections.eli5: The trick is simple and easy, but only works well if everyone is honest and the network is small. Big networks need better planning and routing protocols instead.
